5377.t: Related to Ancient Greek ἠλέκτωρ (ēléktōr, “shining, brilliant; byname of the Sun”), with further origin unknown.

5385.t: Ultimately, the term derives from the root *sweyd- (“to sweat”), whence also ἰδίω (idíō) and ἶδος (îdos)).

5399.t: Possibly from *Holbʰ- 'cry, lament'. Compare ὀλολύζω (ololúzō), ὀλολυγμός (ololugmós).

5372.t: Unknown. According to Vasmer a cognate to Sanskrit ऋ॒ति (ṛtí, “assault”) and Proto-Germanic *ernustuz (“struggle, fight”).

5369.t: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to become equal, be fitting”), albeit with no certain cognates outside of Greek; Lithuanian vỹkti (“to occur, happen”) has been compared, but the Lithuanian is more likely to derive from *weyk- (“to overcome”),…

5383.t: From Proto-Hellenic [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *wéh₁itis (“twining object”), with remodeling of the suffix like in other tree names (compare ἀκτέα (aktéā, “elder (tree)”) and πτελέα (pteléā, “elm”)).

5341.t: The ending is similar to other bird names, like αἰγυπιός (aigupiós), αἰγωλιός (aigōliós) and χαραδριός (kharadriós). The resemblance with Latin ardea (“heron”) and Serbo-Croatian róda (“stork”) cannot be coincidental.

5300.t: No certain etymology. Maybe from the same source of Proto-Germanic *linþaz (“pliable”) and Latin lentus (“flexible”).

5370.t: Formation like δρύοψ (drŭ́ops, “woodpecker”), on an onomatopoeic basis. Parallel names exist in other languages, like Latin upupa, Persian پوپو (pôpô), Armenian հոպոպ (hopop) and Latvian pupukis.

5311.t: Based on φ/π variation with the likely-related ἄφνω (áphnō, “suddenly”), Beekes and Furnee assume Pre-Greek origin, noting that the correspondence of -ιφ-/-πι- suggests that the original Pre-Greek term was pronounced with a *pʸ.

5305.t: The form is similar to κενεός (keneós), but has no clear etymology. Brugmann connects the word with εὖνις (eûnis), but this claim is refused by Kretschmer.

5392.t: The formation is reminiscent of ὕδερος (húderos) and χολέρα (kholéra), but further details are unknown.

5371.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₁wreǵ- (“to close, enclose”). Cognate with Sanskrit व्रज (vrajá, “wattle, fence”) and Middle Irish fraig (“interior wall”).

5379.t: Uncertain. Often combined with ἴπτομαι (íptomai, “to press hard, oppress”), but this is semantically difficult.

5353.t: From ἐν- (en-) + κεῖμαι (keîmai). Serves as the passive of ἐντίθημι (entíthēmi).

5395.t: From Biblical Hebrew יָאִיר (Yāʾîr). Doublet of Ἰαΐρ (Iaḯr).

5352.t: From the same stem as ἐγγύη (engúē, “pledge, surety, security”), which see.
